kh:body.kh:document-title: The FCA Consumer Duty—application to mainstream consumer credit lenders
kh:body.kh:mini-summary: This Practice Note considers the application of the Consumer Duty to MCCL firms, and includes details of the scope of the Consumer Duty’s application to MCCL firms, the interaction of the Consumer Duty with pre-existing FCA rules and guidance, the implications for MCCL firms in complying with the cross-cutting rules under the Consumer Duty, the implications for MCCL firms in delivering the four consumer outcomes under the Consumer Duty, areas of potential difficulty for MCCL firms, implications for MCCL firms in implementing the Consumer Duty for closed products, and practical Consumer Duty steps post implementation.
kh:body.core:para: Firms in the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA’s) mainstream consumer credit lender (MCCL) portfolio, known as MCCL firms, provide unsecured overdrafts, loans or credit cards which are regulated under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 (CCA 1974). The Consumer Duty presents particular implementation challenges for MCCL firms which are explored in this Practice Note.
This Practice Note considers the application of the Consumer Duty to MCCL firms, and includes details of:

core:listitem.core:para: the scope of the Consumer Duty’s application to MCCL firms
the interaction between the Consumer Duty and pre-existing FCA rules and guidance
the implications for MCCL firms in complying with the cross-cutting rules under the Consumer Duty
the implications for MCCL firms in delivering the four consumer outcomes under the Consumer Duty
areas of potential difficulty for MCCL firms
the implications for MCCL firms in implementing the Consumer Duty for closed products, and
practical steps for MCCL firms in embedding the Consumer Duty

kh:body.core:para: The deadline for compliance with the Consumer Duty for new and existing products and services, ie those products or services which are still on sale to new customers or available for renewal by existing customers, was 31 July 2023.

The deadline for compliance with the Consumer Duty for closed book products and services, ie those which were entered into prior to 31 July 2023 and which are no longer on sale to new customers or available for renewal by existing customers, was 31 July 2024. For MCCL firms closed products cover, for example, personal loans entered into before 31 July 2023 on which customers continue to make payments where the firm no longer offers personal loans.

For further information on the main elements of the Consumer Duty with general application, and developments and the implementation timeline, see Practice Notes: The FCA Consumer Duty—essentials and The FCA Consumer Duty—timeline.

tr:secmain.core:title: Scoping issues for mainstream consumer credit lenders—Customers in scope of the Consumer Duty

tr:secsub1.core:title: Credit agreements with 'retail customer'
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 2A.1.5 GThe Consumer Duty applies to products and services offered to ‘retail customers’ (including prospective customers). For consumer credit related activities a retail customer is defined in the FCA Handbook Glossary of definitions as a 'customer' under the FCA Handbook Consumer Credit sourcebook (CONC). Therefore, the Consumer Duty applies to all regulated credit-related activities, including MCCL firms entering into regulated credit agreements for overdrafts, loans or credit cards as lender.

PRIN 2A.1.5 GThis means that the Consumer Duty applies to credit-related activities with natural persons and also with partnerships of fewer than 4 partners not all of whom are bodies corporate ('small partnerships') and unincorporated bodies which do not consist entirely of bodies corporate (and are not partnerships). For regulated article 3(i)(b) credit agreements, the Consumer Duty applies to natural persons acting for purposes outside their trade, business or profession. In relation to consumer credit related activities, the Consumer Duty therefore applies to MCCL firms' dealings with prospective and existing customers who fall within these categories.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Exempt credit agreements with retail customers
tr:secsub1.core:para: Activities which fall within an exemption in the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001, SI 2001/544 (RAO), for example, business lending of more than £25,000 to sole traders and small partnerships which is exempt under article 60C(3) of the RAO, are not subject to the Consumer Duty (PRIN 3.2.9G). However, ancillary credit activities in relation to such loans, such as credit broking, debt collection and debt administration, where such activities fall within the regulatory perimeter because they apply to credit agreements (rather than regulated credit agreements), are subject to the Consumer Duty.
For further information on exemptions under the RAO, see Practice Note: Exempt consumer credit agreements under the RAO.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Application of Principle 12 where MCCL firms provide regulated and exempt credit agreements
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 3.2.10RTo the extent that the Consumer Duty Principle 12 (a firm must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers) applies, Principles 6 (a firm must pay due regard to its customers and treat them fairly), and 7 (a firm must pay due regard to the information needs of its clients and communicate information to them in a way which is clear, fair and not misleading), do not apply. This means that MCCL firms carrying out both regulated and unregulated lending can continue to apply Principles 6 and 7 in relation to borrowers in their unregulated business but must apply the higher standards of Principle 12 (as supplemented by the rules in PRIN 2A) to their dealings with retail customers under their regulated lending business. For example, Principles 6 and 7 continue to apply to exempt business loans for more than £25,000 to sole traders and small partnerships and loans to corporates and larger corporates but the Consumer Duty Principle 12 applies to regulated personal loans.

In practice, for strategic and business consistency reasons, MCCL firms carrying out both regulated and unregulated consumer credit lending may decide to apply the higher Consumer Duty standards to their dealings with all their customers.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Retail customers with closed products
tr:secsub1.core:para: While MCCL firms were not required to apply the Consumer Duty rules in their dealings with customers who have closed products with the firm until the later date of 31 July 2024, MCCL firms could implement the new rules for closed products before that deadline. Depending on various factors, including the proportion of its products which were closed, the remaining term on those products and the resourcing requirements to include the closed book in its implementation plans, a MCCL firm may have implemented the Consumer Duty for its closed products before 31 July 2024 to avoid the complication of having different rules and internal processes applying to their dealings with different groups of customers. A key factor in the decision to implement the Consumer Duty early for closed products might also have been the likelihood of foreseeable consumer harm arising in relation to those products were the new rules not to have been implemented until 31 July 2024.
Consumer Duty implementation challenges specific to MCCL firms' closed products are covered in more detail at Implications for MCCL firms in implementing the Consumer Duty for closed products below.

tr:secmain.core:title: Scoping issues for mainstream consumer credit lenders—firms in scope of the Consumer Duty
tr:secmain.core:para: PRIN 3.2.6RGlossary definition ‘retail market business’PRIN 2A.1.3 GThe Consumer Duty applies to a firm's retail market business only. Under the Glossary of definitions, 'retail market business' covers the regulated activities of a firm in a distribution chain which involves a retail customer. The Consumer Duty therefore applies to all MCCL firms involved in the manufacture, provision, sale and ongoing administration and management of a credit product or service to the end retail customer and those involved in preparing and approving communications that are issued to retail customers.
Where a MCCL firm's retail market business involves operating in a distribution chain:

core:listitem.core:para: PRIN 2A.1.15 Gthe Consumer Duty applies to the extent that the firm is responsible for determining or materially influencing retail customer outcomes, regardless of whether or not the MCCL firm has a direct client relationship with the firm

PRIN 2A.1.14 Gthe extent of the MCCL firm’s responsibilities under the Consumer Duty depends on the firm’s role in the arrangements relating to the product and the extent of its influence over retail customer outcomes

tr:secmain.core:para: Where a MCCL firm's role in the distribution chain is such that it is unable to determine or materially influence retail customer outcomes it may not be subject to obligations under the Consumer Duty.

FG22/5 paras 2.23, 2.24Within a distribution chain, firms are responsible only for their own activities and do not need to oversee the actions of other firms in the distribution chain, unless otherwise required by regulation or contract. If, for example, a MCCL firm's point-of-sale lending product is distributed by a third party alongside retail customers' purchases of goods the MCCL firm is not responsible for ensuring that the distributor is fully compliant with the Consumer Duty. However, if when reviewing its products at a later date, the MCCL firm finds that its loans are not being distributed in accordance with the intended distribution strategy and target market, it must take appropriate action, for example by amending the distribution strategy or providing additional information to the distributor, to mitigate the situation and prevent any further harm.

FS25/2 para 2.25The FCA has confirmed that it will engage with firms to consider how the FCA could provide more certainty on its expectations under the Consumer Duty for firms in retail distribution chains, particularly those who do not interact directly with retail customers. This includes, for example, how firms could share information within the distribution chain and how the Consumer Duty applies proportionately to firms with a more indirect role.

tr:secmain.core:title: Interaction of the Consumer Duty with pre-existing FCA rules and guidance

tr:secsub1.core:title: Overview of changes to the FCA Handbook—Amendments to PRIN
tr:secsub1.core:para: In addition to the new definition of a retail customer, the introduction of the Consumer Duty has resulted in a number of other key changes to the FCA Handbook outlined in this section.
The amendments to PRIN include:

core:listitem.core:para: the introduction of a new consumer principle—the new Principle 12 provides that ‘A firm must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers’. This wording reflects the outcomes focus of the Consumer Duty, which goes further than the existing Principles 6 and 7 (see below on the interaction of Principle 12 with Principles 6 and 7)
A new Consumer Duty chapter (PRIN 2A) setting out:

core:sub1listitem.core:para: cross-cutting rules—these support the Consumer Principle and are set out in PRIN 2A.2. They set clear expectations for firms’ cultures and behaviours, where firms are required to (i) act in good faith towards retail customers, (ii) avoid causing foreseeable harm to retail customers, and (iii) enable and support retail customers to pursue their financial objectives

PRIN 2A.3PRIN 2A.4PRIN 2A.5PRIN 2A.6the ‘four outcomes’—this is a suite of other rules and guidance linked to four particular outcomes that represent the key elements across the whole firm-consumer relationship. The four outcomes underpin the cross-cutting rules. The outcomes relate to (1) the quality of firms’ products and services, (2) the price and value of products and services, (3) consumer understanding and (4) support for consumers

PRIN 2A.8governance and culture rules and guidance—these are required to ensure that the Consumer Duty is embedded in a firms’ governance, strategy and policies, leadership and staff incentives at all levels

PRIN 2A.9monitoring rules and guidance—the retail customer outcomes should be a central focus for firms' risk and internal audit functions, with firms required to monitor retail customer outcomes with record keeping and obligations to notify the FCA PRIN 2A.9
PRIN 3.2.6R–3.2.12Gadditional rules about application (PRIN 3)—these include rules and guidance around scope of the Consumer Duty and the interaction between Principle 12 and Principles 6 and 7

tr:secsub1.core:para: For further information on the elements of the Consumer Duty, see Practice Note: The FCA Consumer Duty—essentials.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Overview of changes to the FCA Handbook—Amendments to the Code of Conduct sourcebook (COCON)
tr:secsub1.core:para: COCON 2.1.6RThe Consumer Duty introduces Individual Conduct Rule 6 requiring Conduct Rules staff to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers. This is applied by:

core:listitem.core:para: COCON 2.4the Consumer Duty Code of Conduct, in line with PRIN 2A

specific guidance on the Conduct Rules (COCON 4) which clarifies that PRIN 2A applies to the whole of the firm, from management to more junior staff, where seniority, expertise and experience are linked to expectations under COCON (ie someone in a management position is more likely to have a greater ability to influence the outcomes experienced by retail customers than someone who is not)

tr:secsub1.core:para: For further information on the Conduct Rules and the FCA’s Code of Conduct for Staff sourcebook (COCON), see Practice Note: Conduct Rules for SM&CR Firms.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Definition of retail customer for consumer credit activities
tr:secsub1.core:para: The Consumer Duty introduces a definition in the FCA Handbook Glossary of ‘retail customer’ for the purposes of the Principles for Businesses (PRIN) and COCON sourcebooks in the FCA Handbook. In these sourcebooks, in relation to activities to which CONC applies, a retail customer is a 'customer' for the purpose of that activity.

As noted in Scoping issues for mainstream consumer credit lenders above, this alignment of the retail customer definition with the definition of customer in CONC means that the Consumer Duty applies to all regulated credit-related activities, including MCCL firms entering into regulated credit agreements for overdrafts, loans or credit cards as lender. MCCL firms therefore have to consider rules in CONC as well as the Consumer Duty rules in PRIN.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Interaction of products and services outcome with pre-existing FCA rules
tr:secsub1.core:para: As the Product Intervention and Product Governance sourcebook (PROD) in the FCA Handbook does not apply to consumer credit products MCCL firms must comply with the products and services outcomes rules in PRIN 2A.3.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Interaction of fair value outcome with pre-existing FCA rules
tr:secsub1.core:para: FG22/5, para 7.55MCCL firms are not currently subject to value assessment requirements under CONC or other Handbook sourcebooks, but under CONC price caps apply for high-cost short-term credit. Where MCCL firms are subject to price caps for high-cost short-term credit the FCA expectation is that they will assess if their charges represent fair value. The price caps should not be seen as a maximum rate that firms can charge; retail customers can still receive poor value when charged within the set price caps. Even where the price caps apply, MCCL firms are expected under the Consumer Duty to assess the value of their products, and this could lead to rates that are lower than the cap.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Interaction of consumer understanding outcome with pre-existing FCA rules
tr:secsub1.core:para: FG 22/5, para 8.72MCCL firms must follow the sectoral rules in CONC and the requirements under the CCA 1974 and related regulations in relation to the provision of information to retail customers as these remain necessary to achieve specific outcomes or to enable retail customers to compare credit products. However, in order to meet the FCA's expectations under the Consumer Duty, MCCL firms need to think more widely about the purpose of their communications in encouraging customers' understanding, and the outcomes they bring about, and this may require MCCL firms to do more than the existing rules require. This is discussed below in relation to CCA 1974-required disclosures, see Consumer outcomes: implications for mainstream consumer credit lenders.

FG 22/5, para 8.18The consumer understanding outcome is wider than the specific CONC or CCA 1974 disclosure requirements and it applies to all communications (including verbal communications). MCCL firms must consider their communications as a whole.

PRIN 2A.5.3 R(2)PRIN 2A.5.3 R(1)PRIN 2A.5.8 RWhile the consumer understanding outcome rules retain the obligation under Principle 7 for firms to communicate information in a way which is clear, fair and not misleading they go beyond the requirements of Principle 7. For example, under the consumer understanding rules MCCL firms must support their retail customers’ understanding by ensuring that their communications meet the information needs of retail customers, are likely to be understood by retail customers intended to receive the communication, and equip them to make decisions that are effective, timely and properly informed. Communications must be tailored taking into account the characteristics of the retail customers intended to receive the communication (including any characteristics of vulnerability), the complexity of products, the communication channel used, and the role of the MCCL firm.
The interaction of Principle 12 with Principle 7 is discussed below.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Interaction of consumer support outcome with pre-existing FCA rules
tr:secsub1.core:para: FG22/5, para 9.56The Consumer Duty does not replace existing FCA Handbook rules that set specific customer servicing requirements, for example providing information or complaints handling. The consumer support outcome sets overarching expectations and in order for MCCL firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers they may need to go beyond existing rules covering specific aspects of the servicing.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Interaction between Principle 12 and Principles 6 and 7
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 3.2.10RPrinciples 6 and 7 do not apply where Principle 12 applies. The implications of this for MCCL firms is discussed above, see: Scoping issues for mainstream consumer credit lenders.

PRIN 2A.1.17 GPRIN 2A.1.17 G(2)There is, however, overlap between Principle 12 (and the wider Consumer Duty) and Principles 6 and 7 and the six treating customers fairly (TCF) outcomes. A failure to act in accordance with existing guidance on Principles 6 and 7 which would have amounted to a breach of those Principles, is likely also to be a breach of Principle 12. Pre-existing guidance on Principles 6 and 7 remains relevant to MCCL firms in considering their obligations under the Consumer Duty but the FCA's expectations under the Consumer Duty go beyond the pre-existing guidance.
Guidance at PRIN 2A.1.17G highlights some of the differences between Principle 12 and Principles 6 and 7. For example, Principle 12:

core:listitem.core:para: imposes a higher and more exacting standard of conduct than Principles 6 and 7. For example, Principle 6 requires firms only to treat their customers fairly while Principle 12 goes beyond this by requiring a firm to deliver good outcomes for retail customers

has a broader application than Principles 6 and 7 in relation to a firm’s retail market business and has a greater focus on consumer protection outcomes for retail customers, irrespective of whether they stand in a client relationship with the firm. For example, Principle 12 applies to firms in the distribution chain even where they have no contractual relationship with the retail customer

tr:secsub1.core:para: A MCCL firm acting in accordance with guidance on Principles 6 and 7 should not rely on this alone when considering how to comply with Principle 12. MCCL firms need to consider what further action they need to take to meet the obligations and FCA's expectations under the Consumer Duty. Material based on Principles 6 and 7, which predates the Consumer Duty, may, however, be useful to MCCL firms when considering their overall obligations under the Consumer Duty.

CONC 7.3.2GCONC 2.10.10GCONC contains both rules and guidance which refer to Principles 6 and 7, or which set out what the FCA expects under Principles 6 and 7. For example, MCCL firms dealing with customers in arrears difficulties should pay due regard to their obligations under Principle 6 to treat its customers fairly, and in accordance with Principle 6, MCCL firms should take reasonable steps to ensure they have suitable business practices and procedures in place for the fair treatment of customers with a mental capacity limitation. In these circumstances (and others where CONC refers to Principle 6 or 7), where a MCCL firm is dealing with a retail customer within the scope of the Consumer Duty it should act to deliver good outcomes for those retail customers and comply with its obligations under the higher standards of Principle 12 and PRIN 2A.

FS25/2 para 2.30The FCA plans to consult later in 2025 on measures to address confusing, outdated or potentially conflicting FCA Handbook requirements to address outdated references to Principles 6 and 7.
For further information, see Practice Note: Consumer credit: rules relating to arrears, default and recovery.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Review of FCA requirements following the introduction of the Consumer Duty
tr:secsub1.core:para: The FCA is seeking to maximise the benefits of the Consumer Duty. In its Call for Input: Review of FCA requirements following the introduction of the Consumer Duty, published in July 2024 the FCA invited comments on whether it might be appropriate and beneficial to place greater reliance on the Consumer Duty in place of specific FCA rules and guidance. In particular, the FCA is seeking to address potential areas of complexity, duplication, confusion, or over-prescription, which create regulatory costs with limited or no consumer benefit. Another aim of the review is to include appropriate flexibility in the FCA's rules to be responsive to future changes and innovation. In its Feedback Statement FS25/2 (dated March 2025) the FCA sets out its intention to address longstanding concerns from firms about the length and complexity of the FCA’s rules and identifies targeted steps to amend discrete areas of the FCA’s rules. The FCA’s workplan, set out in the Feedback Statement, includes:

core:listitem.core:para: allowing firms more flexibility to tailor customer-facing communications in a way which promotes consumer understanding and allows for more modern customer journeys
giving firms more flexibility in how they apply the FCA’s requirements, so that the FCA regime is more outcomes-focused, and
targeted work to remove or review outdated requirements, or areas of unnecessary complexity

tr:secsub1.core:para: FS25/2 paras 1.5, 2.13 and 2.25Consumer FCA: Duty requirements review: updateThe FCA is committed, alongside HM Treasury’s review of the CCA 1974, to reviewing the financial promotion rules for consumer credit. In Q1 2026 the FCA will consult on removing unnecessary prescription, updating outdated requirements and improving alignment with the outcomes-focused Consumer Duty, with a particular focus on CONC 3.5. The FCA will also discuss whether to review rules on the disclosure of Annual Percentage Rates (APRs) and cost disclosure as part of its CONC 3 consultation paper planned in early 2026.

The FCA confirms in the Feedback Statement that it will engage with firms to consider how the FCA could provide more certainty on its expectations under the Consumer Duty for firms in retail distribution chains, particularly those who do not interact directly with retail customers. This includes, for example, how firms could share information within the distribution chain and how the Consumer Duty applies proportionately to firms with a more indirect role.

tr:secmain.core:title: Cross-cutting rules: implications for mainstream consumer credit lenders
tr:secmain.core:para: This section discusses the implications for MCCL firms in complying with the cross-cutting rules under the Consumer Duty. The Consumer Duty includes three cross-cutting rules which set out how firms should act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers:

core:listitem.core:para: act in good faith towards retail customers
avoid causing foreseeable harm to retail customers
enable and support retail customers to pursue their financial objectives

tr:secmain.core:para: The cross-cutting rules articulate the FCA's expected standards of conduct under Principle 12 and work together as a package such that poor conduct will often breach more than one of the cross-cutting rules.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Act in good faith
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 2A.2.2 RFirms must act in good faith towards customers. This is a standard of conduct characterised by honesty, fair and open dealing, and consistency with the reasonable expectations of retail customers.

When retail customers deal with MCCL firms, there is generally an imbalance in bargaining position, knowledge and expertise. MCCL firms must act openly and with honesty so that retail customers can take responsibility for their choices and decisions. MCCL firms must act in good faith at all stages of the customer journey and during the whole lifecycle of a product or service.

PRIN 2A.2.3 G(b)–(c)Manipulating or exploiting behavioural biases to create demand for a product, or taking advantage of a retail customer or their circumstances, for example any characteristics of vulnerability, in a manner which is likely to cause detriment are examples of where a firm is not acting in good faith. Accordingly, MCCL firms should not rely upon targeting vulnerable consumers or exploiting consumer behaviour and biases to create a product that relies on late payment fees or repeat borrowing. Similarly, a MCCL firm which provides credit cards would not be acting in good faith if it seeks to exploit customer inertia and does not communicate clearly and engagingly with retail customers approaching the end of an incentivised rate on their credit card so they can make appropriate and informed financial decisions.

A MCCL firm can act in good faith to support their customers’ understanding by presenting information in an even-handed way that properly explains the benefits and risks of a credit product. MCCL firms should not seek to manipulate consumer choice by making information about certain of their lending products more prominent or more easy to access than others. For example, a MCCL firm which provides credit cards would not be acting in good faith if it presents retail customers with incomplete, distorted or skewed information such as the credit card's cash advance features without explaining with sufficient prominence that the retail customer would be charged interest from the time of withdrawal.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Avoid causing foreseeable harm
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 2A.2.8 RA MCCL firm must avoid causing foreseeable harm to retail customers.

PRIN 2A.2.10 GMCCL firms must avoiding causing reasonable harm at all stages of the lifecycle of the product, including all aspects of the design, terms, marketing, sale of and support for their products and must not unfairly exploit characteristics of vulnerability held by retail customers.

Firms must also take appropriate action to mitigate the risk of actual or foreseeable harm, for example, by amending the product design or distribution strategy. For example, at the product design stage, MCCL firms providing risk-based pricing on credit products should act to avoid foreseeable harm by assessing whether their charges represent fair value to different groups of retail customers, and by taking appropriate action, such as amending charges, where a value assessment identifies that the price of the product or service does not provide fair value to any such group of retail customers. Similarly, where a MCCL firm monitoring a loan product discovers much higher than anticipated default rates and arrears it should assess the information and may as a result review the target market, consider amending the product terms and/or refreshing information and communications about the product.

PRIN 2A.2.10 GThe rising cost of living will impact MCCL firms as increasing numbers of prospective customers may apply for consumer credit, and increasing numbers of existing consumer credit customers might experience financial difficulties. MCCL firms must respond to these emerging trends that identify new sources of harm in order to mitigate actual or foreseeable harm. MCCL firms should also ensure that staff are adequately trained to manage calls, that there are appropriate forbearance options to support consumer needs and that communications are clear. For further information see Practice Note: Responsible lending requirements—CONC 5.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Enable and support
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 2A.2.14 RPRIN 2A.2.23 G(1)MCCL firms must act to enable and support retail customers to pursue their financial objectives. This rule applies throughout the customer journey and lifecycle of the product or service, and applies to prospective customers (even where they do not eventually become customers).

PRIN 2A.2.21 GWhere a MCCL firm declines to provide a retail customer with a credit product, the firm should still consider whether in the light of the financial objectives of the retail customer there is information or support it could provide to help the customer pursue their financial objectives. For example, a MCCL firm could signpost either the ‘Money Helper’ guide to such a customer or other independent and reliable information provided by another third party.

PRIN 2A.2.20 G(1)–(2)MCCL firms can support consumers in pursuing their financial objectives by designing products or services with clear and straight-forward features and having clear communications so the product can be understood by retail customers in the target market and retail customers are able to make informed financial decisions at key points in the product lifecycle. For example, a MCCL firm which provides credit cards can enable and support retail customers seeking to take up the firm's 0% promotional rate on balance transfers by telling those retail customers prior to application what interest free period they will get, what the balance transfer fee will be and whether or not a failure to make minimum repayments will result in the retail customer losing the promotional rate.

FCA: Our Consumer Duty focus areasWhether or not consumers get enough clear information to support decision-making, particularly when taking out a promotional offer on a credit card, will be the subject of FCA planned work in 2025/2026.

tr:secmain.core:title: Consumer outcomes: implications for mainstream consumer credit lenders
tr:secmain.core:para: This section discusses the implications for MCCL firms in delivering the four consumer outcomes under the Consumer Duty. Reference is made to the FCA's expectations as set out in the FCA’s:

core:listitem.core:para: portfolio letter to MCCL firms dated 3 February 2023 on implementation of the Consumer Duty (FCA portfolio letter)
report entitled 'Consumer Duty Implementation: good practice and areas for improvement' dated 20 February 2024 (FCA implementation report), and
a Dear CEO letter to MCCL firms, High-Cost Lending firms and Credit Unions of 20 March 2024 on FCA strategy for consumer lending (FCA consumer lending strategy letter)

tr:secmain.core:title: Products and services outcome
tr:secmain.core:para: Poorly designed products or products which are distributed widely to retail customers for whom they were not designed are likely to result in consumer harm. Products and services need to be fit for purpose for retail customers to be able to pursue their financial objectives and avoid foreseeable harm.

PRIN 2A 3.4RPRIN 2A.3.4 R(4)PRIN 2A.3.4 R(5)In order to deliver good outcomes MCCL firms must ensure that the design of the product or service meets the needs, characteristics and objectives of retail customers in the identified target market and that the intended distribution strategy for the product or service is appropriate for the target market. MCCL firms must specify the target market for their products at a sufficiently granular level, taking into account the characteristics, risk profile, complexity and nature of the product.

PRIN 2A.3.7 RMCCL firms must also monitor to ensure that the product or service continues to meet the needs, characteristics and objectives of the target market, that the distribution strategy remains appropriate and whether or not the product is being sold outside the target market.

MCCL firms must understand their customers’ credit needs and assess whether those needs are met by the products and services which they provide. For example, the needs of retail customers needing long-term borrowing will not be met by a lending product designed for short-term lending and if a MCCL firm were to provide such a product to these retail customers this could lead to the foreseeable harm of persistent debt, unsustainable borrowing and financial hardship. As set out in the FCA consumer lending strategy letter, the FCA expects firms to agree to refinance only where they reasonably believe that it is not contrary to the consumer's best interests to do so (CONC 6.7.18 R).

PRIN 2A.3.4 R(3)MCCL firms must take account of any particular needs of retail customers with characteristics of vulnerability Where a MCCL firm's target market for a credit product includes customers who are likely to be less financially resilient the firm should closely monitor the incidence of late payments, particularly where these incur fees. Good practice, where substantial numbers of customers are making late payments, would be to identify the root cause and where appropriate review creditworthiness criteria, and, for existing customers experiencing financial difficulties, consider amending payment terms to make payments more manageable. Additional support and tailored communications may also help prevent further harm to affected retail customers.

PRIN 2A.3.4 R(4)(ii)MCCL firms offering rate-for-risk loans must ensure that the design of the product does not adversely affect groups of retail customers in the target market, including groups of retail customers with characteristics of vulnerability.

Where a MCCL firm is in a distribution chain they should identify all other parties, (including credit brokers and debt management firms in the chain) and should, along with others in the distribution chain, (including those broking finance), consider their respective roles in the distribution chain and obligations under the Consumer Duty, depending on whether they are acting as manufacturer, co-manufacturer, or distributor.

PRIN 2A.3.3 R(6)Where a MCCL firm's credit products are distributed by credit brokers, the MCCL firm must take all reasonable steps to ensure that the products are distributed to the retail customers they were designed for.

PRIN 2A.3.11 RIf a MCCL firm collaborates with credit broker firms on matters such as the APR price-point, they must have a written agreement outlining their respective roles and responsibilities in the product approval process rules at PRIN 2A.3. The agreement should confirm the roles of the firms and their responsibility for meeting different aspects of the rules under this outcome.

MCCL firms responsible for distribution of credit products and services should identify risks in their incentive structure and manage them to help ensure it does not drive behaviours that result in poor customer outcomes. For example, MCCL firms’ controls for sales targets and staff incentives should identify risks that need managing to prevent mis-selling of financial products.

The products and services outcome does not apply to closed products in the same way as for new or existing products. For closed products there will be no further sales so, for example, there are no requirements for MCCL firms to have a target market or distribution strategy for those products. More detail of the Consumer Duty requirements for MCCL firms' closed products is set out at Implications for MCCL firms in implementing the Consumer Duty for closed products below.

tr:secsub1.core:title: FCA expectations
tr:secsub1.core:para: MCCL firms' key working document for the products and services outcome is likely to be a customer characteristics, needs and objectives needs matrices. These matrices need to identify the target market for products in sufficient detail. The matrices should be set with reference to, and considered in light of, the product or service provided.

When identifying their target market MCCL firms also need to have particular considerations for identifying retail customers who do not follow the typical characteristics and ensure that the products are appropriate for these retail customers with adapted customer journeys being considered. The FCA expects specific journeys for vulnerable customers, for example.

The FCA portfolio letter identifies as circumstances where retail customers are more exposed to foreseeable harm as retail customers experiencing or anticipating repayment difficulties, retail customers whose products are coming to the end of an incentivised rate and retail customers who are repeat borrowing or looking to consolidate debt. It would be appropriate for MCCL firms to consider and identify these separately in their retail customer matrix. The FCA is likely to scrutinise these cases in particular to ensure that products and services are appropriate and deliver good retail customer outcomes. This is separate from a retail customer assessed as showing typical characteristics and needs and who subsequently experiences repayment difficulties. Firms do however need to consider the typical customer journey through the life of the product or service. The FCA portfolio letter makes it clear that extra care needs to be taken when products are sold outside the original target market. Particular concern is raised around extending products to retail customers with poorer credit scores or retail customers facing financial stress who may be more susceptible to purchasing unsuitable credit products.

The Consumer Duty means MCCL firms need to have a far greater understanding of their retail customers' needs and characteristics going well beyond the requirement to assess affordability. Capturing sufficient customer information to ensure that a MCCL firm can meet its Consumer Duty requirements is essential and onboarding information should be reviewed with this in mind.

MCCL firms may also have historic data in respect of their retail customers. MCCL firms may review such data and use it where appropriate. Other means by which data can be obtained is through customer surveys and is a means of continually reviewing delivery of good customer outcomes. Products can be adapted where necessary to take account of market changes, but information obtained may also assist in ensuring that products and services are made available to the target market.
The FCA implementation report sets out observed good practice and highlights areas for improvement.
Examples of good practice identified in the FCA implementation report include firms:

core:listitem.core:para: defining with particular care the target market for products that could cause harm if sold to the wrong consumers, redesigning sales journeys to be clearer on the types of customers and needs products are appropriate for, and introducing new products to meet different customer needs

improving their data and monitoring capabilities to track customers who have bought a product but fall outside the target market so firms can contact them or take other measures to avoid consumer harm
adapting products, for example introducing controls to limit exposure to financial loss, to deliver additional benefits for their customers
making positive changes to their product development processes, including, for example, making more use of consumer research and testing to help ensure products work well, and

simplifying their product offering to remove duplicates of similar products with similar or overlapping features, where this benefits customers, for example by making it quicker and easier for consumers to identify and access the products they need

tr:secsub1.core:para: Examples of areas for improvement identified in the FCA implementation report include firms:

core:listitem.core:para: not sharing information effectively across supply chains

not paying sufficient attention to ensuring that their distribution strategies are driving good customer outcomes. For instance, if a lender firm finds third-party brokers are not distributing its loans in line with its intended distribution strategy and target market, it must consider appropriate action. While the firm is not responsible for the activities of third-party brokers (save where CONC 1.2.2 R applies), it may, for example, need to provide additional information to brokers to ensure the loans are sold to the right borrowers

tr:secsub1.core:title: Further updates
tr:secsub1.core:para: FCA: Payments Consumer Duty multi-firm reviewA finding from the FCA’s multi-firm review of payments firms, which has relevance for MCCL firms is the need to define the target market with care. The FCA noted that a widely defined target market can be appropriate in some circumstances, for example, with low-risk products designed to meet the needs of a broad range of consumers. However, an inappropriately widely defined target market could mean that firms will not identify the true risk of their product or service delivering poor outcomes to consumers. An inappropriately wide definition also makes it more difficult to identify potential harm caused to customers if the products and services are not the right fit. High and medium-risk products are likely to require narrower, well-defined target markets to reduce the risk of harm and avoid customers being sold products that do not match their risk appetite.

tr:secmain.core:title: Price and value outcome
tr:secmain.core:para: PRIN 2A.4.1 RThe price the customer pays for a product or service needs to be reasonable compared to the overall benefits. Value needs to be considered in the round and low prices do not always mean fair value.

PRIN 2A.4.8 RA MCCL firm's assessment of whether or not a product provides fair value must include consideration of a number of factors including the benefits that will be provided or may reasonably be expected, any limitations that are part of the product and the expected total price expected to be paid, which includes the repayments under a credit product, any regular charges or fees payable over the product lifetime and any contingent fees or charges such as arrears charges.

PRIN 2A.4.9 GMCCL firms should carry out a review and value assessment of their pricing models, including interest rate charged, late payment, refinancing and cancellation fees, charges related to the application for or drawing down of the credit, transmission of credit or changing the payment date, so they can demonstrate that their products provide fair value to their customers, taking into account matters such as the costs to the firm in manufacturing the product, market rates and charges for comparable products. Customer research and management information should support this value assessment.

FG22/5 para 7.25For example, where a MCCL firm provides a regulated buy-now-pay-later product at 0% interest with a target market including retail customers on low incomes or with poor credit ratings and significant revenue is generated from default fees the FCA would expect the firm to consider whether elements of the pricing structure could cause foreseeable harm. The MCCL firm should also be able to demonstrate that the overall costs that retail customers are likely to pay, including potential default fees, are reasonable relative to the benefits.

Where a MCCL firm's distribution strategy includes credit intermediaries they should factor average intermediary fees in their value assessments and must also ensure that distributors have the necessary information to carry out their own assessment of value.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Different retail customer groups
tr:secsub1.core:para: FG22/5 para 7.27When designing charges and charging structures, MCCL firms must consider how their target market is likely to use the product or service. Where a MCCL firm has different groups of retail customers with different needs and characteristics, they must also consider the likely price different groups will pay through the expected term of the product relative to the benefits they receive.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Risk-based pricing
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 2A.4.9 G(1)FG22/5 para 7.26PRIN 2A.4.11 GIn assessing value MCCL firms may take into account the costs incurred to manufacture or distribute the product. The price a MCCL firm charges may be high because it reflects the underlying costs to the firm, for example where the retail customer presents a higher credit risk. MCCL firms may charge a higher price to such retail customers than for other retail customers representing a lower risk, but must be able to demonstrate that the benefits were reasonable relative to the price for each group of customers.

PRIN 2A.4.9 G(2)FG22/5 para 7.27Where MCCL firms charge high rates of interest for higher credit risk retail customers they must also consider other elements of the Consumer Duty which may be relevant (see PRIN 2A.4.12G). For example, where a MCCL firm provides a loan on risk-based pricing they should consider whether characteristics of vulnerability or lack of other credit options may make retail customers more at risk of accepting these terms, and also whether the risk of retail customers getting into payment difficulties might be increased as a result of the high loan repayment cost. MCCL firms could consider the credit risk of their customer base and market rates for comparable products as relevant factors, but should consider whether high prices designed to mitigate losses from high default rates in effect facilitate lending which exposes retail customers to a high risk of harm.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Differential pricing
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 2A.4.11 GFCA: Price and Value Outcome: Good and Poor Practice updateThe price and value outcome rules do not require MCCL firms to charge all retail customers the same amount. It also does not prevent cross-subsidies between different groups or services. Differential pricing between new and existing customers, for example an incentivised initial rate, or a discounted rate for credit card balance transfers, in the form of clear, transparent up-front discounts for either set of retail customers is not prohibited. However, where firms charge different prices to different groups of retail customers, they must consider whether the price for the product/service gives fair value for customers in each pricing group, while having regard to whether any customers who have characteristics of vulnerability may be disadvantaged (and being particularly alert to risk that cross-subsidies may disadvantage vulnerable customers).

tr:secsub1.core:title: FCA expectations
tr:secsub1.core:para: A key tool for the price and value outcome is a value-to-cost calculator which should be used to demonstrate the link between the pricing of the MCCL firm's product or service and its benefit to the retail customer and when looking at individual retail customers' circumstances and affordability calculator. MCCL firms have their own pricing models and should build up or enhance existing value assessment frameworks.

The FCA portfolio letter identifies as an area which is likely to be in the spotlight in a FCA review is where different prices are charged to different consumer groups for the same product or service. The FCA portfolio letter highlights that the MCCL firm must ensure that there is for each group of retail customers a reasonable relationship between the price they are paying and the benefit they receive over time and that each group must receive fair value. When setting prices it will become more likely that a clear reason for pricing groups differently needs to be recorded and product pricing for each group needs to show fair value. Factors which firms can consider when assessing fair value include benefit or utility to customers, costs and market rates for comparable products
The FCA portfolio letter identifies two areas under the price and value outcome which MCCL firms should carefully consider to ensure compliance:

core:listitem.core:para: making sure that retail customers' characteristics are not being exploited: The example given is where retail customers are effectively locked-in to a MCCL firm because they would have difficulty getting credit elsewhere possibly due to poor credit history. MCCL firms should consider and be in a position to demonstrate how they have addressed this particular point. The charging of unjustifiably or unreasonably high fees or rates of interest to groups, such as those with a poor credit history, might indicate exploitation

affordability assessments for both initial and increased credit are adequate and accurate so as to avoid retail customer harm: Affordability assessments are not new but it is clear that they need to be sophisticated enough and accurately completed to allow the MCCL firm to take account of particular retail customer circumstances

tr:secsub1.core:para: An assessment of value covers a range of considerations including pricing. FCA guidance (FG22/5 ) makes it clear that assessment of value goes well beyond this aspect and MCCL firms need to consider the wider question of value to the customer.
Examples of good practice identified in the FCA implementation report include firms:

core:listitem.core:para: reducing costs for consumers to improve value, for example by updating pricing models and reducing the rate of interest paid on certain credit products and/or for certain types of customers, reducing or removing charges for certain products or ongoing services where these were deemed too high relative to the benefits provided and putting controls in place for certain groups or customers, for whom charges over a certain amount do not offer fair value, to improve value and remove these charges
enhancing the benefits of products to improve value
considering whether the customer receives fair value across the distribution chain, for example by ending agreements with distributors where firms are concerned about value to the customer
taking steps to monitor or close products where their value proposition risks causing poor customer outcomes.

tr:secsub1.core:para: Examples of areas for improvement identified in the FCA implementation report include firms:

core:listitem.core:para: failing to show that products offer fair value to retail customers, for example by relying solely on an assessment of similar product offerings in a market. Qualitative reasoning outlining why a firm considers that its product offers fair value is required
adding fees along the distribution chain that might mean the overall cost to the end consumer does not represent fair value.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Further updates
tr:secsub1.core:para: In relation to price and value, Sheldon Mills, FCA Executive Director, Consumers and Competition in a speech delivered in February 2024 commented that the equivalent of a 'Google Shopping search does not prove to [the FCA] that a customer is getting a fair deal’ (see FCA publishes Consumer Duty speech and good practice guidance, LNB News 20/02/2024 58). Good benchmarking against comparable firms and products can be a starting point for fair value assessments but fair value assessments need to rely on solid data and other credible evidence to justify a product's value to retail customers. Price benchmarking against the market rather than considering a fuller range, including the real value a customer derives compared to the price they pay, is insufficient in itself to show fair value.

In September 2024 published an update on good and poor practice in relation to the price and value outcome. This update was based on the regulator’s supervisory activity on price and value in the cash savings, GAP insurance and platform cash areas, but the general findings were for all sectors to consider. In the update the FCA’s key messages to firms were that:

core:listitem.core:para: the outcomes of the Consumer Duty should be considered holistically. The price and value outcome should be considered alongside the other Consumer Duty outcomes and cross-cutting obligations, and not in isolation. For example, a product or service that does not meet any of the needs of the customer it is sold to, causes foreseeable harm, or frustrates their objectives, is unlikely to offer fair value to that customer, whatever the price. Conversely, a product or service that meets all of the other elements of the Consumer Duty is more likely to offer fair value. Poor practice could, therefore, include looking at a price level alone without checking customer understanding for the potential harm. Where there is significant risk of consumers not receiving fair value, a firm should identify this risk and consider appropriate mitigating actions, which might include adjusting the core features of a product, ensuring there are alternatives available, effectively communicating with and supporting consumer so they have the right products, and monitoring how these actions are cumulatively working together to ensure customers are receiving fair value

effectively identifying target markets helps in assessing impacts on different customers. Defining the product group and target market for a product are the basic building blocks of a good fair value assessment. Firms should consider the types of customers who, by virtue of their circumstances or behaviours, are likely to get value from the product (inside the target market) as well as the types who are less likely to get value (outside the target market). If different products or services have different features or target markets, they should be considered separately

an analysis of any cross-subsidies can be helpful in identifying where different consumer groups may be at risk of not receiving fair value. Firms must demonstrate that all groups of customers get fair value from their products, and must be alert to risks that cross-subsidies may disadvantage vulnerable customers, and
evidence is vital in fair value assessments, but firms should be proportionate in their approach. The extent

tr:secsub1.core:para: The extent or level of detail of the supporting evidence should be proportionate to the size of the firm and complexity of the factors being considered.

Prompt action should be identified if fair value assessments show that customers are at risk of not receiving fair value and there should be subsequent tracking of the effectiveness of action taken. Where communications are used as a mitigating action, these must be targeted and monitored for effectiveness. Firms writing to customers receiving poor value on their products should set out the actions which the customer might want to take to receive better value, for example considering alternative products offered by the firm that might be better suited to the customer’s circumstances.

FCA: Price and Value Outcome: Good and Poor Practice updateGood practice could include nudging those customers identified using transactional data as not using the product in line with its intended use with targeted communications, and monitoring customers who subsequently transfer to more suitable products. Good practice might also involve reducing or removing charges for some products where they are deemed too high relative to the benefits provided.

tr:secmain.core:title: Consumer understanding outcome
tr:secmain.core:para: PRIN 2A.5.3 RMCCL firms must support retail customer understanding so that their communications:

core:listitem.core:para: meet the information needs of retail customers
are likely to be understood by retail customers and
equip retail customers to make decisions that are effective, timely and properly informed

tr:secmain.core:para: Each of these elements is discussed below.

PRIN 2A.3.4 R(1)Meeting retail customers' information needs: to know their retail customers' information needs MCCL firms must know their target market with sufficient granularity, considering the characteristics, risk profile, complexity and nature of the product or service.
Understandable communications: MCCL firms need to ensure that communications are understandable by the intended recipients.
PRIN 2A.5.7 GIn order to support consumer understanding through its communications MCCL firms should:

core:listitem.core:para: explain or present information in a logical manner
use plain and intelligible language and explain the meaning of any unavoidable jargon or technical terms as simply as possible
make key information prominent and easy to identify, including through use of headings and layout, display and text font, and use of tables, bullets, graphs and other design devices

tr:secmain.core:para: PRIN 2A.5.6 R(1)MCCL firms should consider how the way in which information is presented can help to improve or inhibit understanding, and should ensure that key information is clear, visible and accessible—not hidden within a large volume of material, or hard to find on a website.

The FCA guidance (FG22/5) encourages layering of information as a way of making communications clearer and more effective. Layering is where key information is provided upfront with cross-references or links to further detail. The key information is likely to include any action required by the retail customer and any consequences of inaction. For example, where a retail customer of a MCCL firm is coming to the end of an incentivised rate, key information would include details of the options available to the customer (for example moving a credit card balance to another provider offering an incentivised rate on balance transfers) and the consequences, including increased payments and/or interest rate, of taking no action.

Equipping retail customers to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions: effective communications enable retail customers to evaluate their options by assessing the benefits, risks and costs associated with those options, and how those options relate to their needs and financial objectives.

PRIN 2A.5.6 R(2)MCCL firms should ensure that communications are well-timed and at appropriate touch points throughout the product lifecycle, such as towards the end of promotional rates on a credit product, giving retail customers an appropriate opportunity to take in the information and, where relevant, assess their options. This approach will help to put retail customers in a position where they can make effective decisions on an informed basis.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Tailored communications
tr:secsub1.core:para: PRIN 2A.5.8 R(1)MCCL firms must also tailor communications provided to retail customers taking into account the characteristics of those customers, including characteristics of vulnerability. Firms should follow FCA guidance for firms on the fair treatment of vulnerable customers.

For example, where a MCCL firm has identified that the recipients of a communication being sent to retail customers in arrears may be in financial difficulty and therefore at increased risk of harm if the communication is overlooked or misunderstood, good practice would be for the MCCL firm to tailor the communication. Tailoring could involve including a prominent message in plain English inviting customers to get in contact with the firm if they need help to understand the communication or would like to discuss their options or the support available.

FG22/5 para 8.38Where a MCCL firm identifies different information needs of different groups of retail customers—for example retail customers in, or more likely to fall into, financial difficulties within a wider group of borrowers, firms should consider segmenting or targeting communications to make them more relevant to the intended recipients, rather than adopting a ‘one size fits all’ approach. This will help retail customers to make effective decisions and pursue their financial objectives.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Disclosure requirements under the CCA 1974
tr:secsub1.core:para: The consumer understanding outcome presents a particular challenge for MCCL firms as consumer credit legislation prescribes disclosure requirements which are not always easy to understand (further information on such requirements can be found in Practice Note: Consumer credit agreements—pre-contract requirements).

Respondents to the FCA's December 2021 consultation on its detailed rules and final proposals on the Consumer Duty (CP21/36) expressed the opinion that some existing disclosure requirements do not support consumer understanding. The technical and inflexible nature of certain disclosures prescribed under CCA 1974, s 55 led to these disclosures being regularly cited as problematic.

PS22/9 para 8.7As the purpose of these legislative and regulatory disclosure requirements is to ensure that consumers are provided with certain information to help them make effective decisions at key points in the customer journey the FCA has stated that firms should continue to comply with these requirements. However, MCCL firms must consider the wider purpose of their communications, and the outcomes they are focused on, to meet the FCA's expectations under the Consumer Duty. MCCL firms must ensure that all their documentation presents information in a way which can be understood by retail customers and provides the right information at the right time to enable retail customers to make informed, good decisions. If compliance with other disclosure requirements under the CCA 1974 requires the communication of complex information, MCCL firms should consider what additional steps they can take to support consumer understanding.

In this situation, layering can be used to provide context or to explain key information upfront in a simple way. A cover letter, for example, signposting more detailed information that retail customers may want to consider or for reference at a later date may assist retail customer understanding. Communications must be clear and provide retail customers with the information they need at all stages in the consumer journey where there is potential for consumer harm, for example where retail customers of MCCL firms miss repayments or are in default.

While some disclosure requirements set a prescribed way in which key information about products and services must be presented, in other areas firms have discretion to decide what this key information is or how to explain it. Where MCCL firms have this discretion, they should follow the high‑level rules and guidance under the consumer understanding outcome.

FG22/5 para 8.19Good practice where prescribed communications might be confusing (as might have been the case in relation to notices of sums in arrears in the Covid-19 pandemic when payment deferrals were allowed) would be for MCCL firms in this type of situation to include suitable explanations with or within the statutory notices.

The FCA’s review of the retained provisions of the CCA 1974 (cited in CP21/36) recognised the possible merit in modernising the tone and language used and adopting a less prescriptive and more outcomes‑focused approach to information requirements in some areas. This was followed by the publication of HM Treasury’s ‘Reforming the CCA 1974: Consultation’, on 9 December 2022, which is the first step in the latest major reform of the CCA 1974 (announced in June 2022), with the ultimate aim of moving the majority of the CCA 1974 from statute to FCA rules. HM Treasury believes that this will mean that consumer credit regulation will be more dynamic and futureproof by allowing the FCA to take a ‘test and learn’ approach to regulation. However, as HM Treasury conceded, this consultation was only the first milestone in a process that is expected to take several years (to the extent that it is now taken forward by the new government) and will require legislation to implement. For further information, see Practice Note: Consumer credit—essentials — Reform of the FCA consumer credit regime.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Testing communications to support understanding
tr:secsub1.core:para: MCCL firms should test communications where appropriate. This testing should check communications can be understood by retail customers, so they can make effective decisions and act in their interests.

PRIN 2A.5.12 GApproaches to testing will vary depending on MCCL firms' different size, resources, and activities. When considering if testing is required, MCCL firms should take into account a variety of factors including the purpose of the communication and in particular if it includes key information designed to prompt or inform a retail customer decision, and the scope for harm if the information being conveyed were misunderstood or overlooked by retail customers.

FCA: Payments Consumer Duty multi-firm reviewAs regards ways of testing customer understanding, good practice examples of testing arrangements include testing consumer understanding both before and after communications are sent out and communications using A/B testing, which involves testing particular wording that is different in two otherwise similar versions of a communication to determine which is easier to understand.

Whether or not MCCL firms need to test mandatory CCA 1974 disclosures will depend on the role the disclosure plays in the firm’s overall approach to ensuring retail customers understand key information or risks, including whether or not the MCCL firm is providing additional layered material.

tr:secsub1.core:title: FCA expectations
tr:secsub1.core:para: The FCA portfolio letter highlights the importance of MCCL firms supporting retail customers in their understanding of the options available to them in their decision-making where retail customers are experiencing or anticipating repayment difficulties, coming towards the end of an incentivised rate, and repeat borrowing (or consolidating borrowing).

MCCL firms should review their communications to make sure the communications enable retail customer understanding from point of sale through the life of the product. Communications need to contain sufficient information to allow the retail customer to make an informed decision.

In addition to reviewing communications, MCCL firms could also test understanding through customer feedback and survey responses as well as monitoring whether or not retail customers make anticipated decisions. Unexpected retail customer decisions might indicate that the product is not sufficiently well understood by those customers.

The timing of the provision of information is noted by the FCA. In particular, retail customers are to be provided with information when they need it. Communications across all media should be reviewed to ensure that retail customers are supported in their understanding of options available to them and in their decision making, particularly at key decision points, such as when a credit card incentivised balance transfer rate is coming to an end.

While FCA rules set out the information which must be given to retail customers in payment difficulties, firms have to look beyond compliance with those rules and test, monitor and adapt to ensure retail customers' understanding and good outcomes.

Facilitating ease of access to information and delivering communications through channels that fit best with retail customers means that, where necessary, MCCL firms need to consider and adopt varied means of communication with retail customers in order to meet the requirement to ensure customer understanding.
Examples of good practice identified in the FCA implementation report include firms

core:listitem.core:para: engaging with experts to improve their communications across different channels and increase customer understanding of their products and services, for example through changes to layout and presentation of content, simplifying language used and using ‘jargon busters’, and improving the accessibility of websites, making it easier for customers to get details for further support

considering how their marketing of products such as loans could exploit customers’ behavioural biases, and taking steps to provide more balanced information and moderate its incentivisation to customers with higher risk profiles

redesigning customer journeys, focusing on how consumers behave in practice and risks of harm, for example by identifying where customers could be subject to fees and charges and adding prompts and push notifications during the customer journey to advise of these costs
updating customer interaction points and materials, such as call centre scripts, and delivering training so that staff are better equipped to support customer understanding
being more proactive with their communications to support better customer outcomes
developing ways to test customer understanding such as surveys, experiments, and interviews and monitoring the impact communications have on behaviour.

tr:secsub1.core:para: An example of an area for improvement identified in the FCA implementation report includes firms being unclear with customers about what charges apply, and when. One way to improve customer understanding is to provide worked examples of product and service costs.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Further updates
tr:secsub1.core:para: FCA: Our Consumer Duty focus areasIn September 2025 the FCA announced that it has planned work focusing on consumer understanding in the credit card market. The FCA will focus on how consumers understand the terms and conditions of credit card products and whether they get enough clear information to support decision-making, particularly when taking out a promotional offer.

tr:secmain.core:title: Consumer support outcome
tr:secmain.core:para: MCCL firms should provide support that avoids causing foreseeable harm and enables customers to fully utilise the products and services they purchase and to pursue their financial objectives PRIN 2A.6 R.

PRIN 2A.6 RMCCL firms must provide the support throughout the lifecycle of a product or service after the point of sale—for example to support a retail customer wishing to make an enquiry, claim, complaint or to switch provider. Retail customers of MCCL firms seeking to transfer credit card balances to another provider or to repay their loan early, for example, should be able to do so with the same ease they were able to take out the credit card or loan in the first place.

FG22/5 para 9.10MCCL firms' processes should not cause foreseeable harm to a retail customer. For example, a MCCL firm should consistently record retail customers’ county court judgments as ‘satisfied’ on the Register of Judgments when the judgment has been repaid. This helps to avoid harm to financial health and wellbeing that could arise if these customers were, on the basis of inaccurate information recorded against them, to be rejected for credit products or charged a higher interest rate. Similarly, retail customers seeking to disable a stolen credit card should not be met with unreasonable barriers or frictions that could result in harm.

FG22/5 para 9.22To help avoid financial exclusion and retail customer harm, (for example by retail customers going to illegal money lenders) MCCL firms should have effective declined credit management processes. Where a MCCL firm declines a customer for credit as a result of its affordability assessment good practice would be to signpost them to appropriate information from an independent and reliable source such as the MoneyHelper guide. An example of good practice identified in the FCA consumer lending strategy letter suggests inclusion of an online integrated benefits calculator link to assist retail customers in securing financial support which they are entitled to.

With some retail customers faced with rising living costs more likely to have difficulties meeting loan commitments, MCCL firms may also be able to help customers by signposting available debt help or money guidance. For further information, see Practice Note: Debt advice.

Good practice is for MCCL firms to respond to unforeseeable events which are likely to cause a surge in demand for customer support—for example, a credit card provider might anticipate increased CCA 1974, s 75 claims following the insolvency of a major retailer (see Practice Note: Remedies for connected lender liability in consumer credit). The MCCL firm should have reasonable processes in place to manage increases in demand and be able to dedicate or divert resource to deal with these. An escalation process for urgent issues would allow those matters which are most important to be prioritised.

tr:secsub1.core:title: FCA expectations
tr:secsub1.core:para: The FCA portfolio letter highlights the importance of firms dealing with CCA 1974, s 75 claims appropriately, meeting valid claims and not subjecting retail customers to drawn-out processes which lead to retail customer harm (financial or otherwise). MCCL firms should, where applicable, review their CCA 1974, s 75 claims processes to ensure that valid claims are being met and that there are no unreasonable claims process barriers (also known as friction) which could lead to retail customer harm. MCCL firms should review process flow charts, scripts and statistics around response times, satisfaction times and successful claims in conjunction with information in respect of complaints as part of their assessment of this requirement. The FCA points to poor customer outcomes in relation to section 75 claims during the period of COVID restrictions, which saw a significant growth in section 75 claims, and is looking for MCCL firms to ensure that processes are effective and there are no unreasonable barriers

In periods where economic growth is subject to headwinds with consequences for individuals or consumers are affected by higher inflation or increasing interest rates the numbers of retail customers facing difficult financial and personal circumstances is likely to increase. Retail customers may find themselves unable to meet their repayments under a loan, or may fall behind on their credit card payments, for example. Retail customers in financial difficulty are more likely to have characteristics of vulnerability, and poor treatment of such customers is likely to cause harm. MCCL firms need to provide appropriate support to these retail customers, and this may require different channels or adaptations to firms' usual approaches (for example allowing retail customers to discuss repayment difficulties by telephone rather than automated chatbots).
Examples of good practice identified in the FCA implementation report include firms:

core:listitem.core:para: making changes to ensure the same level of support offered to new customers is available to existing customers

reviewing customer journeys and removing negative obstacles and ‘sludge’ practices that make it more difficult for customers to act in their own interests, for example, removing incentives and changing the way consumers take out credit online, to support better and more active decision making, and enabling customers to exit products through a wider range of channels

introducing positive interventions to customer journeys, for example directing online customers to speak with an agent to receive tailored support where there are indications they may struggle to keep up with repayments, avoiding customers overstretching and setting up unsustainable repayment amounts, and introducing new, flexible repayment plans to support customers struggling to keep up with their credit repayments
creating extra engagement touchpoints with customers to prompt them to make better decisions
taking steps to ensure outsourced consumer support services meet the Consumer Duty standards, and switching provider where appropriate
putting in place processes to monitor the support they provide and identify areas for improvement.

tr:secsub1.core:para: Examples of areas for improvement identified in the FCA implementation report include firms

core:listitem.core:para: not training staff sufficiently well to have complex conversations with customers

not taking the time to understand customer circumstances where they are in financial difficulty, with the potential consequence, for example, that customers do not get a forbearance solution appropriate for their circumstances or advice about other relevant sources of help
having systems that fail to protect and help consumers from loss of personal data due to fraud or cyberattack

tr:secsub1.core:para: In the FCA consumer lending strategy letter the FCA encourages MCCL firms to consider innovation to provide greater access to affordable credit, for example by collaborating with government initiatives such as the No Interest Loan Scheme, offering transparent and competitive interest rates, providing financial education and tools to borrowers, implementing flexible repayment options, and leveraging technology to improve consumer journeys, streamline processes and reduce costs.

tr:secmain.core:title: Areas of potential difficulty for MCCL firms

tr:secsub1.core:title: Risk-based pricing
tr:secsub1.core:para: The FCA has made clear that charging different retail customers different prices for the same product is not in itself an issue. Risk-based credit products continue to be allowed under the Consumer Duty; but for each group of customers, those charged higher prices and those charged lower prices, MCCL firms must be delivering good outcomes, and, in particular each group within the target market must receive fair value. MCCL firms must carefully assess whether the credit product is fair value where retail customers are being charged the highest rates without justification in terms of risk or anticipated cost, and also consider any mechanisms for re-pricing where risk levels change. Risk-based pricing in the context of the products and services outcome is discussed at Consumer outcomes: implications for mainstream consumer credit lenders above.

For high-risk customers, MCCL firms need to consider the likely outcomes, including the consequences of default and arrears, and foreseeable harm. MCCL firms also need to consider whether access to credit is in the interests of certain retail customers.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Getting communications right
tr:secsub1.core:para: For MCCL firms, meeting both the disclosure requirements under the credit regime and the wider requirements of the Consumer Duty is a challenge. MCCL firms should review and monitor their communications to meet the Consumer Duty requirements and the FCA's expectations.
