Where MCCL firms must communicate complex information to comply with other credit regime disclosure requirements, the FCA expects them to consider what additional steps they could take to support consumer understanding. There is an implied recognition that the credit regime disclosure requirements are not always the most readily understandable and an indication that MCCL firms should do what they can to explain in simple terms those matters in the prescribed disclosures which may not engage, or be understood by, the retail customers receiving them. Information overload, however, can deter retail customers from engaging with communications, so MCCL firms must find the correct balance.

As well as reviewing their suite of communications with retail customers and possibly supplementing this with new communications to support retail customer understanding, MCCL firms should closely monitor the effect of these communications on retail customer behaviours and amend where appropriate to achieve greatest engagement and retail customer understanding.

FCA: Payments Consumer Duty multi-firm reviewExamples of good practice consumer understanding testing arrangements include testing consumer understanding both before and after communications are sent out and communications using A/B testing, which involves testing particular wording that is different in two otherwise similar versions of a communication to determine which is easier to understand.
The interaction of the CCA 1974 disclosure requirements with the consumer understanding outcomes are discussed at Consumer outcomes: implications for mainstream consumer credit lenders above.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Customers with characteristics of vulnerability
tr:secsub1.core:para: FG22/5 para 1.27The FCA expects retail customers with characteristics of vulnerability to benefit from the overall improvements in outcomes delivered as a result of the Consumer Duty. Retail customers in financial difficulty are more likely to have characteristics of vulnerability and numbers of retail customers in this situation are expected to increase as a result of the rising cost of living. This could see an increase in retail customers seeking credit products and an increase in retail customers falling behind on repayments. In implementing the Consumer Duty MCCL firms must consider the needs, characteristics and objectives of retail customers with characteristics of vulnerability and follow the FCA guidance on the fair treatment of vulnerable customers (FG21/1) which sets out what firms should do to ensure that those customers’ outcomes are as good as those for other consumers.
Examples of good practice in relation to vulnerable customers identified in the FCA implementation report include firms:

core:listitem.core:para: carrying out a full review of their approach, systems and processes, and centralising operations relating to vulnerability to ensure better outcomes for individual customers through more consistent handling of vulnerable customers by specialist staff,

reviewing their communications and make changes to support vulnerable customers, including, for example, offering literature in alternative formats (such as braille, audio or with enlarged text) and making typographical changes so literature is more engaging (such as by using different colours or fonts)
considering whether information in their communications is appropriate to customer groups with lower financial literacy or where English is not their first language
using customer data to identify potential vulnerabilities (for example, gambling addictions), and sending appropriate communications to those retail customers

improving the way they capture and record information about customer vulnerabilities, for example, using a data flag to identify and monitor outcomes for retail customers who have requested documents in an alternative format.

turning off productivity targets for customer service staff if someone is identified as vulnerable, to encourage staff to take time to provide a bespoke service catered to a customer’s particular needs

tr:secsub1.core:para: Areas for improvement identified in the FCA implementation report include firms:

core:listitem.core:para: not addressing gaps in data and servicing capabilities and failing to address identified weaknesses in processes to track vulnerable customers across multiple product sets
taking a generalised approach to vulnerability, for example automatically assessing all consumers over a certain age as vulnerable, rather than tailoring support to reflect individual needs
asking consumers to self-identify as vulnerable and then unnecessarily requesting evidence of this
asking consumers to disclose their additional needs or personal circumstances repeatedly when passed between teams.

tr:secmain.core:title: Implications for MCCL firms in implementing the Consumer Duty for closed products
tr:secmain.core:para: Chapter 3 of the FCA Non-Handbook guidance (FG22/5) explains how the Consumer Duty applies to closed products and services.

The Consumer Duty applies in full to closed products and services from 31 July 2024, but not to past actions of firms. The way the rules apply to closed products and services is different from how they apply to open products and services. A key difference is in relation to the products and services outcome since, for example, there is no requirement to have a target market or distribution strategy for closed products and services as these are off-sale.
The FCA still expects firms to review closed products and services under the Consumer Duty. This includes:

core:listitem.core:para: reviewing products or services on an ongoing basis under the cross-cutting rules. Firms should actively identify and take appropriate action where they find aspects of, the design of a product or service which means it is not meeting these rules, for example where any aspect of the product or service could lead to foreseeable harm or prevent customers from pursuing their financial objectives
ensuring products continue to offer fair value under the price and value outcome rules
ensuring they meet the customer understanding and support outcomes for closed product customers

tr:secmain.core:para: For closed products certain aspects of the decision to close them may have a bearing on customer outcomes and firms may wish to consider those decisions further, for example if a product was closed because it offered poor value compared to newer products. Firms should prioritise for review those products with a higher risk of consumer harm, for example those products which have attracted customer complaints such as in relation to price and value

In May 2024 the FCA published 6 Dear CEO letters on the implementation of the Consumer Duty for closed products and services (see FCA sends Dear CEO letters on implementing the Consumer Duty for closed products and services by 31 July 2024, LNB News 16/05/2024 78). The Dear CEO letter to consumer finance firms (Dear CEO letter) covered issues such as how firms should consider fair value for closed products and services and how the Consumer Duty applies to vested rights (see further below). The Dear CEO letter also set out priority issues that are particularly acute or widespread in closed products and services as well as action prompts to ensure firms were prepared for the 31 July 2024 deadline.
The 5 priority areas for closed book implementation highlighted in the Dear CEO letter were:

core:listitem.core:para: Gaps in consumer data: firms may not have on file the consumers' characteristics and needs or transaction records, which can make it harder to serve consumers appropriately, particularly those with characteristics of vulnerability. Firms need to take steps to address any material customer data gaps and cleanse and update existing data. The FCA expects firms to evidence that they have taken proportionate steps to fill data gaps or to proactively work around gaps to ensure they are delivering good outcomes for customers. Where a firm cannot fill gaps in its records it should take additional steps to mitigate risk of harm to consumers, for example through enhanced outcomes testing for these customers

Fair value: the fair value outcome applies to closed products on a forward-looking basis from 31 July 2024. Firms' fair value frameworks should be applied consistently to open and closed products and services, and any difference in approach will require justification. The FCA recognises that fair value in closed products is a challenging area and that in some cases customers in legacy products may pay higher charges than they would for open products, where firms are competing for new business. In assessing and demonstrating that their closed products provide value to customers firms can take into account the costs and benefits incurred before the Consumer Duty came into force for closed products

Treatment of consumers with characteristics of vulnerability and customer support: closed products and services may create a particular risk of harm to customers with characteristics of vulnerability, for example, data gap challenges, age and complexity of closed products, inflexibility of legacy systems and changed customer needs can lead to risks of harm and require appropriate levels of care. Firms should consider whether enhanced action, monitoring or support is needed compared to open products

Gone-away or disengaged customers: lack of engagement with customers can lead to problems such as customers paying for products they no longer need or want, customers paying for products they are no longer eligible for and customers not being aware of key changes to products over time, meaning they may not be able to use the products as expected. The FCA still expect firms to go further to drive good outcomes for these customers. Firms should identify less engaged and gone-away customers of closed products and services and take appropriate action, including in relation to how these customers are supported and the communications with these customers. Firms need to be able to evidence why a particular course of action was taken with regard to these customers. Firms should consider whether they have followed all reasonable and proportionate ways of contacting gone-aways and unresponsive customers, and also consider the effectiveness of their activities and channels to contact gone-aways. Firms need to test, monitor and adapt their communications approach if customers communications are not driving the right outcomes for customers. Processes for when gone aways contact firms should also be in place

Vested contractual rights: vested rights – which could include annual fees or exit charges – are also a challenge for closed products. Sometimes these terms enshrined in vested rights can lead to poor outcomes for closed product customers, for example if a fee is significant and undermines the benefits of the product. Some firms might take the view that giving up a vested right and reconsidering fees or charges is the best way to deliver good outcomes for their customers. Where firms have a vested right which they do not wish to give up they should consider alternative ways to prevent or manage foreseeable harms for existing customers, for example through clear communications on what other deals are available and support on how to switch products

tr:secmain.core:para: As was the case for the implementation for open products and services the FCA's expectations with regard to any areas of non-compliance is that firms should prioritise areas where there is the greatest level of harm or potential harm and consider whether that harm might be affecting vulnerable customers. Firms should have in place clear mitigations to protect customers from harm or potential harm in the period until identified improvements have been fully implemented.

tr:secmain.core:title: Practical Consumer Duty steps post implementation—Monitoring
tr:secmain.core:para: Following implementation of the Consumer Duty MCCL firms must review on an ongoing basis the requirements in respect of their products and services. This requires an assessment of evolving retail customer needs and characteristics and ensuring that the Consumer Duty remains embedded in MCCL firms' culture, governance and processes. Staff are likely to have training requirements on their roles with their firms in relation to the Consumer Duty and these need to be identified and updated on a regular basis.

As the Consumer Duty is intended to improve outcomes for all retail customers, MCCL firms must use monitoring to identify where distinct groups of retail customers, such as customers with characteristics of vulnerability, get worse outcomes than other retail customers.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Different outcomes for different groups of retail customers
tr:secsub1.core:para: Where a MCCL firm using risk-based pricing considers that distinct groups of retail customers receiving different outcomes is compatible with the Consumer Duty it must be able to stand behind and evidence this conclusion. In particular, a MCCL firm must be able to demonstrate that the pricing for its products is, and remains, fair for each group.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Use of data to evidence good outcomes
tr:secsub1.core:para: In order to monitor their delivery of good retail customer outcomes MCCL firms need to collect and analyse data. MCCL firms should be collecting information which enables them to assess if certain groups of retail customers, such as those with characteristics of vulnerability, are receiving worse outcomes than other groups of retail customers. The type of information MCCL firms use will vary depending on their size, client base, and the types of credit products or services they offer.

FCA: Delivering good outcomes for customers in vulnerable circumstances – good practice and areas for improvementMCCL firms that collect relevant data to make evidence-based assessments of their customers’ experiences are likely to be better able to understand whether they are delivering good outcomes, and can use this data to inform their approach to improving outcomes.

For example, when monitoring delivery of good outcomes for retail customers around the price and value outcome, possible types of data which MCCL firms could use include the expected price paid by retail customers, (including associated fees and charges) and profitability data, (including revenue and profit margins).

In relation to the consumer understanding outcome, where MCCL firms must ensure retail customer understanding of prescribed information and notices, MCCL firms might use behavioural insights in relation to customer communications to identify barriers to customer engagement or understanding, and to monitor the engagement with additional explanations and communications which MCCL firms produce to improve customer understanding of prescribed information and notices.

MCCL firms should also consider drawing on external sources of data about consumer outcomes. For example, the Financial Lives survey contains date at a granular level about the financial lives of different groups, which might help MCCL firms better understand their retail customers' needs and characteristics, particularly retail customers with characteristics of vulnerability as a result of financial pressures or with low financial resilience, and assess whether or not they are delivering good outcomes for each group of their retail customers.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Identification of root cause of poor retail customer outcomes
tr:secsub1.core:para: MCCL firms must investigate the root cause of poor retail customer outcomes and address any problems. For example, where a MCCL firm's monitoring reveals high rates of late payments and high levels of late payment fees on a personal loan, for example, it must analyse this information to assess the root cause. Creditworthiness assessments for new retail customers may have to be reviewed, additional support and communications may be required to support existing retail customers, and where the target market includes retail customers with characteristics of vulnerability, such as low financial resilience, the MCCL firm must pay particular attention to mitigating the risks to which those retail customers are exposed.

Good practice around root cause analysis includes firms creating post analysis action plans with clearly designated owners, deadlines and remediation actions (which could include staff training or process changes), and reviewing the effectiveness of the implemented solutions.

FCA: Complaints and root cause analysis: good practice and areas for improvementGood practice also includes the adoption of the ‘Five Whys’ problem-solving technique to encourage deeper thinking and to challenge assumptions about the root cause of a problem. An example of this practice given by the FCA relates to a customer being declined a loan on the basis of a credit score which did not meet the lender’s requirements.

tr:secmain.core:title: Practical Consumer Duty steps post implementation—FCA messaging
tr:secmain.core:para: MCCL firms should follow closely any Consumer Duty messaging from the FCA, including on its website, via additional guidance, speeches and Dear CEO letters (all of which can be found on the The FCA Consumer Duty—timeline) and take action where required. As the new rules continue to bed in MCCL firms can expect further communications from the regulator to address implementation matters and eventually more business as usual matters.

FCA: Our Consumer Duty focus areasIn September 2025 the FCA announced that it has planned work focusing on consumer understanding in the credit card market. The FCA will focus on how consumers understand the terms and conditions of credit card products and whether they get enough clear information to support decision making, particularly when taking out a promotional offer.

tr:secmain.core:title: Practical Consumer Duty steps post implementation—Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) decisions
tr:secmain.core:para: As the Consumer Duty continues to bed in, and the approach taken by the Financial Ombudsman Service becomes clearer, MCCL firms should take future as well as existing decisions and guidance from the ombudsman service into account and apply the same approach to similar cases. The FCA has indicated that it will consider a firm which delays paying redress due where the FOS has made a decision relevant to the firm's particular case.

Consumer FCA: Duty requirements review: updateThe FCA has been working closely with the FOS and HM Treasury to produce a set of proposals designed to align the FOS and the FCA on the interpretation of FCA rules. The FCA has indicated that in H1 2026 it will share a ‘strong package of measures’ including changes to the legislative test by which the FOS determines cases and the introduction of formal referral mechanisms to improve coordination and consistency in the redress system. A joint policy statement with the FOS in Q1 2026 and further consultation are planned.
